title: Photosynthesis, Respiration, and Cycles in Nature
competency: Explain the role of plants and animals in the cycles of nature, such as the carbon, oxygen, and water cycles; describe the process of photosynthesis and respiration, and identify its raw materials needed and products.
objectives: Identify the raw materials and products of photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
Identify the cell organelles where photosynthesis (chloroplasts) and respiration (mitochondria) occur.
Explain how photosynthesis and respiration are complementary processes.
Describe the role of organisms in the carbon, oxygen, and water cycles using flow charts.
introduction: Energy and matter are never lost in an ecosystem; they are continuously recycled. Plants capture solar energy to produce food through photosynthesis, while both plants and animals release that energy through respiration. These biological processes drive the great cycles of nature—carbon, oxygen, and water—that keep our planet alive.
content:
1. Photosynthesis: Capturing Energy

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants (producers) convert light energy into chemical energy (glucose). It occurs in the Chloroplasts, specifically within the green pigment called chlorophyll.

  • Raw Materials: Carbon Dioxide (CO2), Water (H2O), and Sunlight.
  • Products: Glucose (C6H12O6) and Oxygen (O2).
  • Equation: CO2 + H2O + Light Energy → Glucose + O2

2. Cellular Respiration: Releasing Energy

Respiration is the process by which cells break down glucose to produce energy in the form of ATP. This occurs in the Mitochondria (the powerhouse of the cell).

  • Raw Materials: Glucose and Oxygen.
  • Products: Carbon Dioxide, Water, and ATP (Energy).
  • Equation: Glucose + O2 → CO2 + H2O + ATP

3. The Complementary Relationship

Photosynthesis and Respiration are opposites. The products of photosynthesis (glucose and oxygen) are the raw materials for respiration. Conversely, the products of respiration (CO2 and water) are the raw materials for photosynthesis. This creates a perfect cycle of matter.

4. Cycles in Nature

  • Carbon-Oxygen Cycle: Plants take in CO2 for photosynthesis and release O2. Animals breathe in O2 for respiration and release CO2.
  • Water Cycle: Plants contribute to the water cycle through transpiration (releasing water vapor from leaves), which eventually leads to condensation and precipitation.

examples.title: Starch Test in Leaves
examples.description: Scientists use iodine to test for the presence of starch in a leaf. A blue-black color indicates that the leaf has successfully performed photosynthesis and stored the glucose as starch.

examples.title: Aquariums
examples.description: In a balanced aquarium, the plants provide oxygen for the fish, while the fish provide carbon dioxide and waste (nutrients) for the plants.

keyTerms.definition: The organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place.
The organelle where cellular respiration occurs to produce ATP.
Adenosine Triphosphate; the primary energy carrier in all living organisms.
Tiny pores on the surface of leaves that allow gas exchange (CO2 in, O2 out).

keyConcepts: Photosynthesis stores energy in food; respiration releases energy from food.
Chloroplasts are found only in plants, but mitochondria are found in both plants and animals.
The balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is maintained by the cycling of these processes.
summary: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are the two most important biological processes on Earth. While photosynthesis builds glucose using sunlight, respiration breaks it down to fuel life. Together, they ensure that carbon, oxygen, and water move continuously between living organisms and the environment.
